blocks.title: Track the unit of transfer and who controls it
paragraphs: Memory organization maps logical addresses and word widths onto physical storage. DMA changes who performs a sequence of transfers; interleaving changes which bank handles successive addresses. Keep these questions separate.
All size calculations below state whether an address counts bytes or words. A capacity in bits is not an address count until the addressable unit is known.

blocks.title: DMA moves the transfer loop out of the CPU
paragraphs: With programmed I/O, the CPU performs the transfer operations. Interrupt-driven I/O can avoid continuous status polling, but the CPU may still move each item. DMA lets a controller carry out a configured block transfer between a device and memory.

The CPU sets up the transfer and handles its completion or errors. DMA still uses memory/bus resources, so CPU and DMA activity may contend for bandwidth. It does not mean the CPU has no setup work or that memory accesses become free.

blocks.title: Build depth and width independently
paragraphs: Build 2048 words of 16 bits using chips of 512 words by 4 bits, with exact depth/width multiples. Four chips in parallel provide 16 bits per addressed word. Four depth groups provide 2048 word positions, so 16 chips are required.

Each chip needs nine address pins for its 512 words and four data pins. The board uses eleven word-address bits: nine within a depth group and two selecting a group. Control, power and ground pins are excluded from these address/data counts.
Capacity is 2048×16 = 32768 bits = 4096 bytes of storage. The board’s stated logical addresses are words; do not call its eleven word-address bits a byte-address width.

blocks.title: Split a word address into bank and row
paragraphs: For low-order interleaving across four banks, define bank = word address mod 4 and row = floor(word address/4). Word address 13 maps to bank 1, row 3 because 13 = 4×3+1.

Successive word addresses visit banks 0,1,2,3 in turn. A stride of four repeatedly visits one bank. Interleaving can overlap service across banks, but actual throughput still depends on bank cycle time, requests and bus constraints.

blocks.title: Check units before multiplying
paragraphs: Write the target word count/width and chip word count/width. Compute width parallelism and depth groups separately, multiply for chip count, then cross-check total stored bits.

For a bank problem, first convert a byte address to the specified word address if needed. Apply the declared bank mapping, then analyze conflicts under the given timing rules. Do not assume every access is conflict-free.

blocks.title: Separate capacity from throughput
paragraphs: DMA changes transfer control. Chip organization changes physical capacity/width. Interleaving changes distribution across banks. None alone guarantees a particular execution speed.
Use the organization workbench for chip/pin arithmetic, and Practice for fixed organization/bank cases and an unscored DMA comparison.

cards.prompt: What work remains for the CPU when DMA is used?
cards.answer: It configures the transfer and handles completion/errors. The DMA controller transfers the block, but memory/bus contention and setup costs remain.

cards.prompt: How are chips combined to increase memory word width?
cards.answer: Use chips in parallel for different bit slices of the same addressed word. Depth groups instead add more word addresses.

cards.prompt: How many address and data pins does a chip with 2^a words of d bits need?
cards.answer: a address pins and d data pins in this non-multiplexed organization, excluding control/power pins. Capacity is 2^a×d bits.

cards.prompt: What is the low-order interleaving rule for B banks?
cards.answer: For word address w: bank=w mod B, row=floor(w/B). State the addressable unit and bank mapping explicitly.

cards.prompt: Why can a stride equal to the bank count defeat low-order interleaving?
cards.answer: It preserves the bank index, repeatedly accessing the same bank. Bank service and bus timing determine the actual penalty.

guided.title: Compare transfer mechanisms
guided.prompt: Compare polling, interrupt-driven per-item transfers and DMA for a block of input, without inventing timing numbers.
rubric: Distinguish status detection from who performs each data transfer.
Identify CPU setup/handler work and shared bus/memory traffic.
Explain which additional measurements would be needed for a speed claim. No keyword or automatic numeric score is used.
